clinical_targets.goal: Resolution of heartburn and acid regurgitation
Complete healing of erosive esophagitis and peptic ulcers within 8 weeks
Step down to lowest effective dose or on-demand therapy once healed

steps_summary: Step 1: Initial Healing Therapy (Erosive Esophagitis & Peptic Ulcer)

steps.title: Initial Healing Therapy (Erosive Esophagitis & Peptic Ulcer)
steps.rationale: Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) are the most effective medical therapy for acid suppression and mucosal healing.

drug_classes.role: Irreversibly inhibits H+/K+ ATPase pump in gastric parietal cells.
drug_classes.dosing: Esomeprazole 20–40 mg once daily; Pantoprazole 40 mg once daily; taken 30–60 minutes before breakfast for 4–8 weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Must be taken before food for maximal efficacy. Pantoprazole has the lowest CYP2C19 interaction potential (preferred if on Clopidogrel).

steps.title: Helicobacter pylori Eradication Regimen
steps.rationale: Mandatory in all patients with confirmed H. pylori peptic ulcer disease to prevent recurrent ulceration and gastric malignancy.

drug_classes.role: 14-day regimen; preferred in areas with high clarithromycin resistance.
drug_classes.dosing: PPI BID + Bismuth Subsalicylate 300 mg QID + Metronidazole 500 mg TID + Tetracycline 500 mg QID x 14 days.
drug_classes.pearls: Re-test for eradication with stool antigen or urea breath test at least 4 weeks post-treatment and 2 weeks off PPI.

drug_classes.role: Only acceptable if local clarithromycin resistance is known to be < 15% and no prior macrolide exposure.
drug_classes.dosing: Esomeprazole 20 mg BID + Amoxicillin 1000 mg BID + Clarithromycin 500 mg BID x 14 days.
drug_classes.pearls: Resistance rates in Egypt often exceed 20%; quadruple therapy is generally more reliable.

special_populations.renal_impairment: PPIs do not require dose adjustment in renal impairment. Long-term PPI use has rare associations with acute interstitial nephritis.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Omeprazole and Pantoprazole have extensive safety data in pregnancy. Sucralfate is a non-absorbed alternative for mucosal protection.

style_3_monograph.summary: A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of your stomach or your duodenum, the first part of your small intestine. A burning stomach pain is the most common symptom. The pain: Starts between meals or during the night Briefly stops if you eat or take antacids Lasts for minutes to hours Comes and goes for several days or weeks Peptic ulcers happen when the acids that help you digest food damage the walls of the stomach or duodenum. The most common cause is infection with a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori . Another cause is the long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs) such as aspirin and ibuprofen. Stress and spicy foods do not cause ulcers, but can make them worse. To see if you have an H. pylori infection, your doctor will test your blood, breath, or stool. Your doctor also may look inside your stomach and duodenum by doing an endoscopy or x-ray. Peptic ulcers will get worse if not treated. Treatment may include medicines to reduce stomach acids or antibiotics to kill H. pylori. Antacids and milk can't heal peptic ulcers. Not smoking and avoiding alcohol can help. You may need surgery if your ulcers don't heal. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
style_3_monograph.treatment: Consult healthcare provider for individualized management.
